strengths: Timely and relevant problem: combining explicit Chain-of-Thought decomposition with GRPO-based RL for text-to-motion generation is a reasonable direction that addresses a genuine gap (lack of explicit reasoning/compositionality in end-to-end T2M models).
The MotionCoT Data Engine provides a practical, automated pipeline for generating CoT-style supervision with quality filtering, reducing reliance on manual annotation.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation on HumanML3D against many recent baselines (MDM, MLD, MoMask, MotionGPT, MotionLLM, MotionGPT-2, etc.) with 20-run confidence intervals, and the method achieves competitive or best results on R-Precision@2/3, FID, MM-Dist, and Diversity.
Ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contributions of CoT supervision, semantic reward, and motion similarity reward, showing that rewards are essential for generation quality.
Includes both in-distribution and OOD qualitative comparisons, and discusses limitations honestly (e.g., RL-only training instability motivating cold-start SFT).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of existing components (VQ-VAE tokenizer from T2M-GPT, CoT distillation from DeepSeek-R1, and off-the-shelf GRPO with cosine-similarity rewards). The adaptation of GRPO to motion tokens is straightforward, and the proposed rewards are simple similarity measures. Semantic planning for motion already exists (MotionAgent), and RL for T2M already exists (MotionRL, PPO-based), so the delta over prior work is incremental.
KIT-ML is claimed as an evaluation benchmark, but no quantitative results on KIT-ML are reported anywhere in the paper (only HumanML3D Table 1); this is a completeness and consistency issue.

The Diversity score of 10.026 (nearly matching ground-truth diversity) combined with a reward that directly compares generated motions to ground-truth motions raises a reward-hacking/memorization concern; the paper does not address whether high Diversity reflects genuine one-to-many generation or mode-matching to the training set. MModality (2.317) is not clearly superior, and the claim of 'significantly outperforms all methods on Diversity' deserves scrutiny.

Reported improvements over the closest competitor are small (e.g., 1.19% diversity and 2.12% R-precision over MotionAgent, and differences vs. MoMask/MotionGPT-2 in FID/R-Precision are within or near confidence intervals), yet the abstract/introduction claims 'state-of-the-art performance.' No statistical significance tests are provided.

The OOD advantage—arguably the central motivation of the paper—is only supported qualitatively through cherry-picked visual examples; there is no quantitative OOD benchmark (e.g., compositional splits, human study ratings), making the core claim about compositional reasoning hard to verify.
No quantitative comparison with MotionRL [47], the most relevant RL-based T2M baseline, despite citing it.

Several details needed for reproducibility are missing from the main paper: group size G, KL coefficient beta, clipping epsilon, training iterations, codebook size N and downsampling rate l, SFT vs. RL data sizes, and how the CoT text conditions generation (it appears the CoT is only used as SFT/RL scaffolding, but its role at inference is not clearly described).

The ablation table (Table 2) is confusingly formatted—rows with checkmarks for CoT/Rsem/Rmotion are ambiguous (e.g., which row corresponds to which subset), and the text interpretation ('All ablated variants achieve comparable performance') contradicts the large gaps shown.

Writing/consistency issues: MotionDiffuse is cited as both [38] and [45] with duplicate references; several references are incomplete (e.g., [20], [27], [47] lack venue/year); diversity improvement described as '1.19%' although Diversity is not a percentage; a claim of 'fair comparison' is asserted without detailing whether baselines were re-run or numbers copied.

No analysis of the actual CoT outputs at scale (e.g., whether reasoning traces correlate with motion quality, or failure modes of LLM-generated plans), so the interpretability claim remains largely unsupported.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely question: whether explicit Chain-of-Thought-style decomposition and group-relative RL (GRPO) can improve text-to-motion generation, which is a reasonable and under-explored combination.

The two-stage training recipe (SFT cold-start on LLM-generated CoT traces followed by GRPO with format, motion-similarity, and semantic-similarity rewards) is clearly described and includes an honest observation that pure RL from scratch is unstable in this setting.

The automated MotionCoT annotation pipeline is a practical contribution that reduces reliance on manual annotation, and the ablation study provides some evidence that CoT plus reward shaping jointly matter.
Standard benchmark protocols (HumanML3D, KIT-ML) and 20-run 95% confidence intervals are used, with a reasonable set of VAE-based and diffusion-based baselines.
weaknesses: Incomplete evaluation: the abstract and Section 4 claim evaluation on both HumanML3D and KIT-ML, but no KIT-ML results table is presented anywhere in the manuscript. This is a material gap that weakens the empirical claims.

Marginal and overstated improvements: the headline gains over the closest baseline (1.19% diversity, 2.12% R-precision vs. MotionAgent) are small and arguably within practical noise; Motion-R1 is not the best on several metrics (e.g., FID 0.201 is worse than MotionGPT-2's 0.191; R-Precision@1 merely ties MoMask), yet the paper repeatedly claims 'state-of-the-art performance'.

Unsupported central claim: the core motivation is that CoT reasoning improves compositional, long-horizon, and out-of-distribution instruction following, but this is supported only by a handful of cherry-picked qualitative figures (Figures 1 and 4). No compositional/OOD benchmark, no user study, and no metric that directly measures multi-step or reasoning fidelity is provided. The FID/R-precision metrics cannot substantiate the reasoning claims.

Ablation study is confusing and internally inconsistent: the text claims 'enabling CoT alone results in the poorest performance', yet the best row requires all three components and the reward-only rows (rows 4-6 of Table 2) collapse to near-random performance (Top-1 ~0.32-0.37), suggesting the ablations conflate training instability with component contributions. It is also unclear how the semantic/motion similarity rewards are even computable without a functioning generation pipeline in the reward-only configurations.

Limited novelty: the pipeline is a fairly direct combination of existing ingredients (VQ-VAE tokenizer as in T2M-GPT/MotionGPT, DeepSeek-R1-style CoT distillation, off-the-shelf GRPO, and similarity rewards analogous to prior multi-reward RL work such as MotionRL). The extension of GRPO to motion generation is described as a contribution but involves no algorithmic modification.

The GRPO/reward description is technically muddled: the paper states rewards 'are not directly used in scalar form but are reflected through groupwise preference ranking', yet Eq. (3) explicitly uses scalar rewards r_i in the normalized advantage; how multiple rewards are aggregated is never specified.

Reproducibility is weak: key hyperparameters (group size G, KL coefficient beta, learning rates, training steps, tokenizer configuration such as codebook size and downsampling rate) are missing from the main text; the CoT prompt and supplementary details are referenced but not included. The 'project page' placeholder on page 1 is empty.

The quality-control loop for CoT data (DeepSeek-R1 judging its own outputs for 'relevance, conciseness, and logical coherence') is described only superficially, and no statistics on the generated dataset (size, filter rate, example diversity) or analysis of CoT quality-vs-outcome correlation are provided.

Several citation/reference hygiene issues: entries [15], [27], [45], [47] lack venues and years, references [20] and [21] have no venue information at all, MotionDiffuse appears twice under different numbers ([38] and [45]), and in-text attribution errors exist (e.g., Section 4.3 discusses 'MotionLLM [9]' while [9] is MotionAgent).

Qualitative claims about MotionLLM failing specific OOD prompts ('fails to complete a full circle', 'produces repetitive or generic motions') are presented without quantitative backing or multiple seeds/samples, which risks cherry-picking.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: bringing explicit Chain-of-Thought-style decomposition and reinforcement learning to text-to-motion generation is a sensible direction that addresses a real limitation of end-to-end mapping approaches.

The MotionCoT Data Engine is a practical contribution: an automated LLM-based pipeline for generating structured CoT annotations with a quality-control loop reduces reliance on manual labeling and could be useful to the community.

The paper is generally well organized and clearly written; the two-stage SFT + GRPO training recipe is described step by step, including a candid discussion of why pure RL training is unstable for motion tokens.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol on HumanML3D (20 runs, 95% confidence intervals) against a broad set of recent baselines (MoMask, MotionGPT-2, MotionLLM, etc.), plus a component-wise ablation study and qualitative OOD examples.
Code, model, and data are promised to be released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overstated claims of state-of-the-art: on HumanML3D, Motion-R1 is not the best method on several key metrics. FID is 0.201 vs. MoMask's 0.045, and R-Precision@1 (0.515) merely ties MoMask. The claimed SOTA rests mainly on R-Precision@2/3 and MM-Dist, which are correlated retrieval-style metrics; the framing exaggerates the evidence.
The KIT-ML dataset is claimed to be evaluated, but no KIT-ML results table appears in the manuscript; only HumanML3D results are reported. This is a significant evaluation gap.

The ablation study (Table 2) is confusing and hard to interpret: the checkmark configuration of each row is ambiguous, and some rows (e.g., the row labeled with only 'Rsem'-like checkmarks) show near-random-level results (R-Precision@1 ~0.32-0.36) that are not clearly explained. The text says 'All ablated variants achieve comparable performance' while simultaneously reporting that CoT-only performs poorly, which is contradictory.

Technical soundness concerns: the motion similarity and semantic similarity rewards (Eqs. 4-5) require the ground-truth motion at training time and rely on pre-trained encoders from [3], which may bias the model toward the evaluation encoder's representation space (the same encoders are used for the reported metrics, raising a risk of metric gaming). The statement that rewards 'are not directly used in scalar form but reflected through groupwise preference ranking' is vague—how multiple rewards are aggregated into a single scalar per sample for GRPO is never specified.

Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe (LLM backbone + VQ-VAE tokenizer + DeepSeek-R1-distilled CoT + GRPO) is a fairly direct transplantation of DeepSeek-R1-style training to a new domain. The contribution over prior MotionAgent (semantic planning) and MotionRL (RL with PPO) is incremental rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Missing details that hinder reproducibility: no information on group size G, KL coefficient, training epochs, RL hyperparameters, VQ-VAE codebook size/downsampling rate, model parameter counts of the final system, or inference cost relative to baselines; the supplementary material with prompts is referenced but not provided.

No quantitative evaluation of the OOD/generalization claims: the central motivation (compositional, long-horizon instructions) is supported only by a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figures 1 and 4) with no quantitative OOD benchmark or human study, so the headline claim that CoT reasoning improves compositional generalization is weakly supported.

Citation and naming inconsistencies: the paper alternates between 'MotionAgent' and 'MotionLLM' while both cite [9] (which is MotionAgent), and there are duplicate/incorrect references (e.g., MotionDiffuse cited as both [38] and [45]), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a coherent overall narrative connecting the two proposed components (Decomposed CoT Data Engine and RL Binding) to the identified challenges.

Evaluation is reasonably extensive: three benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL), comparisons with many recent baselines, 20-run evaluations with 95% confidence intervals, and an ablation study covering each major component.

The system achieves strong results on several metrics (e.g., best R-Precision@2/3, MM-Dist, and Diversity on HumanML3D; best R-Precision and FID on KIT-ML; best across metrics on BABEL), and includes qualitative OOD visualizations.

The paper avoids costly human preference annotations by using embedding-based rewards, and discusses limitations, ethics, and reproducibility; appendices provide prompts, training details, and compute information, which supports reproducibility.
The observation that end-to-end RL training from scratch is unstable for motion token generation (motivating the cold-start SFT stage) is a useful empirical finding.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially the DeepSeek-R1 recipe (SFT cold-start + GRPO with rule/embedding rewards) applied to an existing VQ-VAE + LLM motion generation pipeline. The 'Decomposed CoT Data Engine' is LLM prompting with self-filtering, and 'RL Binding' is a straightforward weighted combination of cosine-similarity rewards; neither is a deep methodological contribution.

Potential evaluation circularity / reward hacking: the motion similarity and semantic similarity rewards (Eqs. 4-5) use the HumanML3D pre-trained text-motion encoder, which is also the evaluator used to compute R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, and Diversity. RL training directly optimizes (a proxy of) the exact evaluation metric, which can inflate reported benchmark numbers without reflecting genuine generation quality. The paper does not discuss or control for this concern, e.g., with a held-out independent evaluator or human study.

SOTA claims are overstated. On HumanML3D, FID is 0.201 vs. MoMask's 0.045 (4x worse); on KIT-ML, MM-Dist (3.196) is actually worse than T2M-GPT (3.007) and MotionLLM (2.982). The '3.5% improvement in MM-Dist' framing is imprecise for a distance metric and obscures non-uniform superiority. The abstract's 'surpassing existing methods across key metrics' does not fully match Table 1.

Missing direct comparisons with the RL-based methods the paper criticizes (MotionRL, MotionCritic) — these are discussed as primary related work and baselines for the 'overly complex RL' claim but are absent from Tables 1-3. Comparisons with other LLM-based reasoners for motion (e.g., MotionAgent) are also absent.

The claim in Section 4.4 that 'All ablated variants achieve comparable performance' contradicts the table, where full-model results are substantially better than all ablations; several ablation rows appear mislabeled or mis-formatted (e.g., rows lacking the CoT checkmark yielding 0.365 Top-1 while CoT-only yields 0.340), undermining confidence in the ablation analysis.

The CoT data generation and quality control both rely on DeepSeek-R1 (generation, relevance/consistency filtering), introducing circularity; no quantitative analysis of CoT trace quality, agreement with human judgment, or the effect of CoT trace length/decomposition granularity is provided. How the CoT trace influences the actual motion generation (which is a single <Motion> token sequence) is not mechanistically analyzed.

Key implementation details are thin in the main paper: which VQ-VAE checkpoint or retraining setup is used, reward weighting coefficients, how the motion encoder differs (if at all) between reward and evaluation, and whether baselines were evaluated under identical settings.

Several writing issues reduce polish: inconsistent dataset counts ('two widely-used benchmarks' listing three), grammatical errors ('In general, our work's contributions can be summarized in the following three folds'), and the claim that Motion-R1's Diversity exceeding ground truth on BABEL 'reflects the ability to synthesize varied yet realistic motions' — higher-than-real diversity is typically a cautionary sign, not a virtue.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (text-to-motion generation) and the idea of injecting structured, decomposed reasoning traces into motion generation is a reasonable direction.
The framework is clearly described at a high level, with a two-stage (cold-start SFT + GRPO) training recipe and reasonably complete implementation details (backbone, hyperparameters, compute).
Experiments cover three standard benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL) with standard metrics and confidence intervals, and an ablation of the main components is provided.
The appendix discloses LLM usage, ethics considerations, and limitations, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Reward–metric circularity undermines the central evaluation claims. Both the semantic similarity reward (Eq. 5) and the motion similarity reward (Eq. 4) are computed with the T2M evaluator encoders from Guo et al. (2022a), which are the exact same encoders used to compute R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, and Diversity at evaluation time. Optimizing cosine similarity directly against the evaluation embedding space makes the reported gains (e.g., the headline '3.5% MM-Dist improvement') largely tautological, and the paper never discusses or controls for this.

The 'state-of-the-art' claims are overstated. On HumanML3D the reported FID of 0.201 is roughly 4.5x worse than MoMask (0.045), a direct baseline in the same table, yet the abstract and Section 2 claim Motion-R1 'surpasses existing methods across key metrics.' Selective emphasis on favorable metrics contradicts the table.

The claimed novelty is limited. The VQ-VAE tokenizer is adopted wholesale from T2M-GPT; the CoT traces are produced by prompting DeepSeek-R1 with the provided template; and 'RL Binding' amounts to a weighted sum of two pre-trained-encoder cosine similarities plus a format check within standard GRPO. This is incremental reward shaping rather than a new algorithmic contribution, and the paper does not compare against the RL baselines it criticizes (MotionRL, MotionCritic).

The role of the decomposed CoT at generation time is unclear. The paper does not explain how multiple decomposed sub-actions are temporally grounded to produce a single continuous motion, nor whether the reasoning traces actually influence the generated tokens rather than serving as formatting overhead. No analysis (e.g., fidelity of generated reasoning steps, or generation conditioned on CoT vs. caption alone at inference) is provided to validate the core hypothesis.

The ablation study (Table 2) is internally inconsistent and hard to parse. The text states 'All ablated variants achieve comparable performance,' which contradicts the table (e.g., Top-1 R-Precision ranges from 0.322 to 0.515, FID from 0.20 to 1.7). The row encoding of the three binary components is ambiguous, some ablated rows show implausible MModality values (>4, above the ground-truth range), and the reported CoT-only FID of 0.530 is inconsistent with the discussed numbers.

Benchmarks comparisons are incomplete and possibly unfair: no MoMask result on KIT-ML, no MotionGPT-2 on KIT-ML, no RL-based baselines anywhere, and no user study or human evaluation to support claims about motion realism and OOD generalization, which rest only on cherry-picked qualitative examples.

Writing and presentation are sloppy, which erodes confidence: the BABEL appendix section is titled 'Qualitative Results on BABEL' but contains quantitative results; MotionDiffuse is cited twice (2022a/2022b) with the same title; the abstract lists 'two widely-used benchmarks' followed by three datasets; and Figure 3's caption is interrupted mid-sentence by body text.

Diversity above ground truth (10.026 vs. ~9.91 on HumanML3D; 8.90 vs. 8.52 on BABEL) combined with the FID behavior suggests the method may be inflating embedding-space statistics (consistent with the reward circularity issue) rather than genuinely improving diversity; this alternative explanation is not analyzed.
The interpretability claim (a stated motivation) is unsupported: no evaluation of whether the generated <think> traces are faithful, accurate, or causally used by the model is provided.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent end-to-end framework (Motion-R1) that combines a Decomposed CoT Data Engine with GRPO-based RL training, and clearly articulates the motivation for each component (cold-start instability motivating SFT, annotation-free rewards motivating RL Binding).

Evaluation covers three standard benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL) with 20-run 95% confidence intervals, and results are competitive: best R-Precision Top-2/3 and MM-Dist on HumanML3D, best R-Precision and FID on KIT-ML, and strong BABEL results (FID 0.53 vs. 1.14 for the best baseline).
An ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contributions of the CoT data engine and the two reward terms, supporting the claim that they are complementary.
The appendix provides prompts, training hyperparameters, compute details, and a limitations section, which supports reproducibility, and code release is promised.
Qualitative comparisons include out-of-distribution prompts targeting the temporal-decomposition motivation, which is directly relevant to the claimed contribution.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'state-of-the-art performance' is overstated. On HumanML3D, Motion-R1's FID (0.201) is substantially worse than MoMask (0.045), and R-Precision Top-1 (0.515) merely ties MotionLLM. The paper selectively emphasizes MM-Dist (a 3.5% gain) while describing FID as merely 'competitive,' which is inconsistent with the abstract and contributions claiming SOTA across key metrics.

Missing comparisons with the very baselines the paper positions itself against: no quantitative comparison with MotionRL (Liu et al., 2024) or MotionCritic (Haoru Wang et al., 2025), the RL-based methods criticized as 'overly complex.' The central claim of a simpler yet stronger RL strategy cannot be verified without these comparisons.

The ablation study has internal inconsistencies. The text states 'All ablated variants achieve comparable performance' in the same paragraph as 'Using the Decomposed CoT Data Engine alone yields the weakest results.' The table layout (which component corresponds to which row) is ambiguous, and it is unexplained that combining Rsem+Rmotion without CoT (0.365) performs worse than either reward alone, which is counterintuitive and unanalyzed.

Novelty is moderate: the core recipe (SFT cold-start with LLM-generated CoT traces followed by GRPO with verifiable rewards) is a direct transplant of the DeepSeek-R1 pipeline to a new modality; the individual components (VQ-VAE tokenizer from T2M-GPT, GRPO from DeepSeekMath, reward encoders from HumanML3D) are all existing, and the decomposition quality control is heuristic.

The CoT traces are generated text-only by an LLM without any grounding in the actual motion content, so the 'reasoning' may not reflect true temporal/causal structure of the ground-truth motion; no analysis is provided of decomposition accuracy or of whether the <think> content actually influences generation (e.g., perturbation tests).
Qualitative evaluation compares only against MotionLLM on a handful of cherry-picked prompts, with subjective assessment and no user study.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the BABEL appendix is labeled 'Qualitative Results' but contains a quantitative table; references are inconsistent (e.g., 'Haoru Wang et al.' listed as first author); minor formatting artifacts appear throughout; the FID on BABEL (0.53) is suspiciously far below all baselines and even below what the KL-regularized RL process would typically achieve, warranting verification of the evaluation protocol.
The claim that RL Binding 'simplifies the optimization process' is asserted but not demonstrated (e.g., no training stability, reward curves, or complexity comparison against MotionRL/MotionCritic).
